IT STARTS WITH a quick glance—a double-take in the mirror under harsh bathroom lighting. Then there it is: a single, wiry hair brazenly peeking out of your nostril like it’s trying to escape. Soon, you’re spotting strands in places they never used to grow, like your ears, and this only multiplies with time. While a beard trimmer, electric razor, or pair of tweezers can help, the best way to keep them in check is to arm yourself with a nose hair trimmer—preferably one that won’t feel like a medieval torture device.

Nose hair trimmers are specifically built to tackle those tricky, hard-to-reach spots. Many models come loaded with extras—think built-in lights, interchangeable heads, even mini vacuums to keep your sink clean. Technically, you could use scissors, but it’s a risk. Snipping near sensitive nasal tissue can lead to nicks and cuts, and as for waxing—well, that’s best left to professionals, not your bathroom mirror. Unless you enjoy excruciating pain and opening your nostrils to infection and disease.

It might be unpleasant to look at when overgrown, but nose hair exists for a reason. It acts as a natural filter, trapping dust, debris, and other particles before they make their way into your body and potentially cause infection or illness. That’s why fully removing it, like with waxing, isn’t a great idea. But those long, visible strands sticking out? They’re not doing the job any better than the hidden ones. The key is balance: trim regularly, but don’t overdo it. Just tidy up when the hairs start to show.

Most nose hair trimmers are reasonably affordable, and shelling out a ton of money isn’t necessarily going to get you the best one. Think about how often you’ll use it, and if you’re mostly concerned with nose hairs or want to use it for other things, too. Many come with multiple attachments to help you tackle errant eyebrow hairs and sometimes even detail your beard. Plus, there are quality nose hair trimmers available at every budget point, so get ready to say goodbye to those long hairs for good.

This is the Rolls-Royce of nose hair trimmers—pricey, yes, but absolutely premium in performance. Its comfortable, well-balanced design lets me use it not just on my nose, but also for my ears and eyebrows. Still, where it really stands out is clearing nasal hair quickly and comfortably. The built-in vacuum keeps things sanitary by reducing leftover clippings and minimizing bacterial buildup.

I also appreciate the wet/dry functionality—it’s easy to clean whether I’m using it in the shower or at the sink. During testing, I found the dual-edge blade trimmed hair much faster than cheaper options, like the Zorami trimmer, which often needed extra time to do the same job. And while the vacuum system is a major plus for cleanup, I did have to empty it about every four months or so with regular use.

Testing Notes: This nose hair trimmer is bulky, per se, because nose hair trimmers are, by default, small appliances, but it is hefty. It sits well in your hand and is easy to hold and grip, which is a surprisingly needed and under-represented feature in the nose hair trimmer world. It’s truly the Rolls-Royce of trimmers, powering through thick and long nose hairs with ease, and leaving your nostrils feeling shorn and clean.

The vacuum is also a very welcome feature that I didn’t know I needed until I tried it. After all, who really wants to clean up nose hair clippings from their sink? The one thing I will say is that while you can technically use this in the shower thanks to the wet/dry feature, cutting hair of all kinds is easier when it’s dry, even nose hairs. I’d recommend sticking to using it outside of the shower.

Long-Term Results: After six months of using Panasonic's Ear and Nose Hair Trimmer, I found that it trims my errant nostril hairs as well as it did right out of the box. The battery life did decrease slightly after six months of using it, but not enough of a decline to make a huge difference.

Battery-powered nose trimmers work fine if you’re only trimming once in a while. But if you stay on top of your nostril grooming (and you should—nose hair grows faster than most people think), a rechargeable model makes way more sense. That’s why I went with this one from Manscaped.

It's not surprising that the brand that reinvented the body groomer delivered the same technology above your neck with the first iteration of The Weed Whacker, but the 2.0 takes it to a whole other level.

It packs a 7,000 rpm motor—the only more powerful option is the Panasonic trimmer, our best overall—into a compact design, and the hypoallergenic stainless steel cone protects sensitive skin while trimming. That means you get a smooth cut without the tugging or irritation.

Testing Notes: During my first time using it, I noticed how seamlessly it cut nasal fur. Even more impressive: it was the quietest trimmer I’ve tried, which made for an even more pleasant shaving experience. Plus, the tip is angled to allow you to reach even the hardest-to-reach crevices in your schnoz.

Unlike most of the other nose hair trimmers on this list, it’s rechargeable via USB, so no need to switch out batteries. Each charge also gets you 45 minutes of trim time, which is the longest on this list. For comparison, Panasonic’s best in-case option gets 40 minutes per charge.

Long-Term Results: After using it for two months, Manscape's marquee nose trimmer cut just as close as it did when I first tested it. Not to mention, its 45-minute battery life still held up after multiple charges.

Read More: Should You Trim Your Nose Hair?

I get it, building a solid grooming arsenal can get expensive quickly. So if you're looking to trim costs (pun intended) on your grooming gadgets, but still want something that gets the job done, then look to Zorami's trimmer that's less than $14. Given that it's a top-rated rig on Amazon, I decided to try the Zorami ourselves.

At this price point, I was impressed by its waterproof capabilities and a 6,500 RPM motor that slices hair pretty cleanly. While it didn't cut as closely as the Manscaped or Philips Norelco trimmers, it still did a commendable job cleaning our nostrils, only adding a few extra minutes to our shaving time compared to our top-rated trimmers.

You can easily pop off the top and rinse under water to clean. Then, after every use, you can snap on the protective top case, a useful feature for keeping your gadget clean while traveling. The only qualms about this trimmer might be overall durability and lifespan, but for those who don't have a lot of nose hair to battle, this is an ideal starter trimmer to go with.

Testing Notes: When you’re using this trimmer, compared to the others on this list, you can definitely tell it’s an inexpensive version. That’s not necessarily a bad thing; it just means that it doesn’t have a lot of the bells and whistles that some of the more expensive options have. That said, it delivers where it matters—namely, cutting ability.

It’s not as fast as some of the others on this list and, in some cases, doesn’t cut quite as close (those with thicker nose hairs will need to use it a bit more frequently), but for the average guy with average nose foliage, it does the job and does it well. The pop-off cap cleaning option is also a nice touch, which makes cleaning it easy to remember.

Long-Term Results: After testing Zorami's trimmer for a month, I noticed a slight decline in cutting ability, and some minor pulling. But the difference wasn't too drastic, and I’d imagine most guys wouldn’t notice.

If you’re looking for an all-in-one trimming option, this Philips Norelco model is pretty hard to beat. Yeah, it doesn't have Panasonic's vacuum feature, but it can still cut nose hair just as effectively, thanks to a dual-sided steel blade that chops down strands without any tugging.

The blades have protective tube technology designed to protect the nostrils from cuts and irritation, making it great for sensitive skin, especially considering the nostrils are one of the most sensitive areas on the face. The nose, ear, and eyebrow attachments (with multiple-length combs) all work well, and the trimmer even comes with a nifty attachment for your sideburns.

Testing Notes: As a nose hair trimmer, this multifunctional tool delivers on everything you want a nose hair trimmer to be. It cuts with ease; it doesn’t pull or snag your hair, and it doesn’t irritate or nick the inside of your nose. The blades are sharp and fast, and the tube housing makes it easy to use.

If you’re into things like eyebrow detailing and other small tweaks to your facial hair, the additional attachments may come in handy, but I found that they are a little trickier to use and not as efficient as the nose hair attachment.

Good thing there is a pouch included, as well, because these attachments are tiny and definitely easy to lose at the bottom of your Dopp kit or bathroom drawer. I usually prefer a rechargeable tool, but the replaceable lithium battery is fine and convenient for travel.

Long-Term Results: After using it for four months, I can safely say that Philips' Norelco trimmer still trimmed just as efficiently as it did when I first received it. While it comes with several attachments for shaving the rest of your body, I found that they didn't cut as closely as the original blade, so I’d recommend buying a separate body groomer.

Most nose hair trimmers use either a rotary blade or a dual-blade setup. What really sets the Conair model apart, though, is its distinctive mushroom-shaped cutting head. The lip at the tip lets me guide it precisely along the inner edge of my nostrils, reaching spots that other trimmers couldn't quite get to. Of all the options I’ve tried, this one gave me the closest trim.

While a lot of people—including many of my fellow editors—really appreciate this unique design, some are perfectly content with a standard rotary trimmer. Honestly, it comes down to personal preference, the way your nose hair grows, and how often you find yourself trimming.

Beyond the cutting performance, I also appreciated the Conair’s ergonomic build. Its textured grip gave me better control, and the slim body fit easily into my travel kit—ideal for keeping things tidy on the go. It also includes three attachments for beard and body grooming, but I found those didn’t shave nearly as close as the nose hair trimmer itself.

Testing Notes: Let’s be honest—the extra attachments are fine if you need them, but they don’t compare to the main attraction: the nose hair trimmer. What really impressed me was its mushroom-shaped head. It’s a smart design tweak that lets me reach spots inside my nostrils that traditional trimmers usually miss.

Long-Term Results: After using it for over five months, I still dig this trimmer’s super close cut. However, Conair's motor has gotten slightly louder over time.

If you’re primarily interested in portability, Wahl’s Micro Groomsman is your best bet. This little gadget packs serious power and efficiency while barely being larger than a Sharpie. Perfect to fit in any travel bag or Dopp kit, the Micro Groomsman will ensure there are no lingering nose hairs poking out, whether you’re departing for the beach or the boardroom.

Its sleek rotary head can smoothly manage nose hairs (not to mention ear whiskers), while its detailer blade adjustment can help shape and neaten facial hair. This add-on also comes in handy for cleaning up necklines and other last-minute touchups when traveling.

Thanks to its streamlined design, operating the device was quick and simple—another boon for busy travelers. While the Micro Groomsman is not waterproof, cleaning it only requires removing the stainless steel rotary head to run it under water.

Testing Notes: I primarily use the Micro Groomsman when traveling or for last-minute touchups in a jam, but it certainly has the power to be an everyday nose hair trimmer, especially for those with less thick hair.

Long-Term Results: The integrity and effectiveness of the Micro Groomsman’s design hold up over time; however, the battery life may leave some wanting more. The batteries don’t last as long as other trimmers on this list, which could prove taxing to last-minute travelers. I initially got about two months of regular use with one fresh battery, but it’s closer to six weeks now, so I’d recommend bringing along a backup battery for any traveling.

Sure, electric nose hair trimmers are probably best for daily grooming, but let’s be real—sometimes these trusty devices just can't get rid of that one stubborn hair. That's when a good pair of nose hair scissors comes in handy to take care of those last few strays.

Of all the scissors I've tried and snipped with, the Shears 3.0 were by far the most effective—and durable. Doubling as nail clippers (though you probably shouldn't use the same pair for both), these shears are sharp enough to eliminate any lingering hairs and tiny enough to fit into the smallest of nostrils. Plus, it comes in a nifty travel kit that includes a fingernail clipper, toenail clipper, nail file, and slant-tip tweezers—all of which are stainless steel and waterproof. It’s a mainstay in my Dopp kit.

Testing Notes: In theory, you could use these scissors to trim all your nose hairs, especially if your nose isn’t too fuzzy. But, honestly, they're best suited for those precise touch-ups—like snipping away a few stray hairs when needed. But either way, take it slow. As these were designed to also trim fingernails, they’re quite sharp and can certainly cause a cut if you're not careful. To limit risk, I recommend you get up close to the mirror and be deliberate, so you're only trimming the hairs you want to get rid of.

Long-Term Results: I don’t use these shears nearly as often as my electric trimmer, since they're best for touch-ups or travel, but they still cut as cleanly as when I first tested them. Thanks to their stainless steel design, there’s been minimal wear and tear over the six months I've been testing them, not to mention zero rusting.

Of course, one of the few complaints about electric nose hair trimmers—battery-powered or otherwise—is often their need to be recharged or refueled with new batteries. This Royal nose hair trimmer combats that common gripe by eschewing electricity entirely.

It works by simply squeezing the handles together, which manually rotates the blades to trim hair. The indented handles also help to ensure you never lose your grip and the tool stays properly placed in your nostril.

The Royal Nose Hair Trimmer is specifically designed to avoid irritation by enclosing blades so that they won’t come in contact with skin, limiting the risk of cuts and nicks.

Sure, the process is slightly more laborious, and the cuts aren’t as precise as other nose hair trimmers on this list, but it’s barely enough to notice. That tradeoff may be well worth it for those who are sensitive to the noisier nose hair trimmer.

Testing Notes: Given its manual design, there were times when this trimmer pulled hair rather than cut it. This can occasionally feel like plucking your nose hairs instead of cutting them, but when operated properly with some patience, it usually holds up without much pulling.

That said, cleaning was a bit more involved than the above options, as you have to pop the top off to do so. The device is water-resistant, however, so you can simply run it under the faucet in a jam.

Long-Term Results: As an everyday nose hair trimmer, this one might not be ideal, but it’s a great option when traveling. I found it can also come in handy during those ever-stressful times when batteries or a charge abruptly die.

When it comes to nose hair trimming, or any manscaping, really, the means by which blades will be brushed against your skin is crucial. For nose trimmers, this typically comes down to one of two options: either a rotary or slide cutter. Slide cutters resemble more traditional clippers, while rotary heads are the ones that look closer to a pen cap. While rotary options tend to give a closer shave, slide cutters offer more control and precision since they only cut in a straight, back-and-forth motion.

Given that these devices are made to be inserted into the nostril, most are primarily equipped with a rotary head, but some offer the option of a slide for folks who prefer the old-school feel. Of course, there are also a few with adjustments for both to accommodate the more indecisive among us.

With most products, you might look solely for a long battery life to ensure you can spend less time charging or replacing batteries, and more time using the device. However, with nose hair trimmers, there are a few other caveats to consider, which can impact the overall grooming experience—namely, the source of its power.

Battery-operated nose hair trimmers take up less storage space, as they don’t need a charging mount or cable, but will likely cost more long-term due to battery replacements. On the other hand, nose hair trimmers with wall chargers can be refueled at any time as long as there’s an outlet nearby. Plus, there are few things more annoying than a trimmer sputtering out with dying batteries, which chargers make easier to avoid. While nose hair trimming takes substantially less time than beard or body hair, you’ll still want one that has at least 30 minutes of runtime to avoid frequently recharging.

At Men’s Health, we’ve been testing nose hair trimmers for years now, focusing on key performance factors like trimming precision, comfort during use, ease of handling, value for the price, and long-term durability. There isn’t a nose trimmer out there that we haven’t gotten our hands on at some point, while also paying close attention to common pain points, like pulling, irritation, and inconsistent results.

While updating this roundup with the latest and greatest nose trimmers, I considered past favorites and emerging tools, ultimately landing on over 20 to try or give another look. After testing each for at least three weeks, I refined our findings to a final shortlist: the eight best nose hair trimmers that truly deliver on performance and reliability.

I’ll admit, the idea of sticking a trimmer up your nose can feel a little intimidating at first, but trust me, the best nose hair trimmers are built to be safe and painless. Most use rotary blades, which are tucked inside a cylindrical guard to protect your skin. That design helps prevent snags and, thankfully, those awful little nicks that hurt way more than they should.

When I trim, I gently place the device just inside one nostril, switch it on, and slowly rotate it to catch as many hairs as possible. There’s no need to push it too far—keeping it shallow is safer and more effective. I usually listen for the sound of hair being cut, and once it goes quiet, I move on to the other nostril.

Some trimmers also come with a slide cutter, which I’ve found more useful for shaping sideburns or cleaning up my neckline. That said, if you’ve got extra-long hairs in your nose or ears, you can carefully trim them down with the slide cutter before switching back to the rotary head for a closer finish.

Also, rest assured that this process isn’t painful with the right tool. Even if you have really long or thick nostril hairs, using a nose hair trimmer won’t hurt. The blades aren’t shaving the hairs down to the skin—they’re just cutting them to a length so they won’t stick out of your nose. Think of it the same as getting a haircut.

Despite their relatively low price, it can still be hard to justify a tool for such a specific issue. Luckily, you can use a nose hair trimmer in some other places. Even the simplest ones are good for ear and eyebrow hairs.

Some other trimmers also come with interchangeable attachments to help shape facial hair and trim mustaches, beards, and sometimes body hair. But keep in mind that if you use an attachment for your nose, you shouldn’t use it anywhere else to avoid cross-contamination. Even if you wash it off thoroughly, it’s a risk.

Still, others are full-on clippers with a nose hair trimmer attachment. Choose one depending on where you want to use it, but don’t try to go rogue. Stick to what the trimmer and attachments are designed for.

#4902. Maximo milestone: friendly robot has completed 300,000 tasks

After completing the first half of Amazon’s Bellefield complex last summer, Maximo engineers have put their helpful robot friend into high gear, with the latest version 3.0 robot-equipped construction crews installing as many as 24 solar panel modules per hour, per person. And now, the company is reporting that Maximo has completed its 300,000th construction task. (!)

If that 24 modules per hour, per person rate sounds fast, that’s because it is. At full tilt, the latest Maximo robot-equipped crews have nearly doubled the output of traditional installation methods at similar solar locations throughout Southern California. Now, with 300,000 tasks under its belt, the robot is proving to be both fast and durable.

“The future of solar construction depends on bringing together the experience of our people and new technology,” explains Matt Tetrault, President of Primoris’ Renewables business.

Like just about everyone these days, Maximo is playing up its machines’ NVDIVIA hardware, re-branding its robots’ repetitive automation as “physical AI.” That’s not to say the robots don’t work, however – as their deployment at Amazon’s Bellefield solar field is proving.

(By) leveraging NVIDIA AI infrastructure together with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries and NVIDIA Isaac Sim open robotics simulation framework, the Maximo team was able to develop, test and refine robotic capabilities through physics-based simulation and AI driven modeling before deploying updates in the field. The combination of AI, vision, robotics and simulation driven engineering reduced development and validation timelines and increased confidence in field performance as the robotic fleet scaled.

Amazon Web Services (AWS) powered the development, deployment, and operation of Maximo’s AI-driven field systems. AWS provides scalable computing, automated software delivery, and advanced data analytics, including real-time construction intelligence, enabling Maximo to collect operational robotics data and continuously improve performance.

The rapid deployment of solar panels at utility scale projects like this one, which is set to eventually reach over a GW of solar generating capacity, will help companies like Amazon reduce their carbon footprint, of course – but also save them big money as the price of fossil fuels continues to climb.

So Primoris’ Renewables is the name of a business, Maximo is the name of a solar robotics company incubated by The AES Corporation. Maximo makes a robot (also called Maximo I think) using NVDIVIA hardware and software, and also AWS cloud software, and Bellefield is a solar field owned by Amazon. Or so I gather so far.

The Maximo team says it has plans to extend its robots potential use cases beyond solar and into construction tasks that require similar pick and place and feeding and attaching movements, site logistics, and site cleanup. And like just about every other business that demands a high degree of physical labor, the construction industry is facing huge labor shortages, making machines like Maximo that provide real efficiency gains welcome additions to the job site.

#4897. The 10 Best Face Washes for Men in 2026, Tested by Grooming Editors

Soaps from Kiehl’s and Tower 28 came out on top in our testing.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

EVERY GOOD SKINCARE routine starts with the same thing—a quality face wash. Before you layer on serums, moisturizers, and eye creams, you need to clear the canvas. A face wash does exactly that by clearing away dirt and grime that accumulate on your skin while also helping prevent clogged pores that can trigger breakouts. That’s why it’s crucial to find the best face wash for you, no matter your skin type.

Wash your face every morning, night, and after heavy workouts to remove bacteria and sebum before they build up, says dermatologistDr. Anthony Rossi, MD. The best face washes for men go beyond cleaning: they hydrate, fight acne, and control excess oil. This first step in your routine is especially important if you live an active lifestyle. While cardio workouts boost circulation and support collagen production, sweat can leave your skin vulnerable to breakouts and irritation.

With so many products out there, finding the right one for your skin type and preferences can feel impossible. That’s why I spent the last two years testing every cleanser I could get my hands on to find the ten best face washes for virtually any skin type and price point.

A face wash is the cornerstone of any skincare routine—without it, the rest of your products won’t work as well. Choose one that’s gentle yet effective because even if your entire routine is just washing your face, you don’t want a cleanser that strips away your skin’s natural oils.

Matching your face wash to your skin type ensures it works with your skin’s natural needs, clears and balances your complexion, and primes your face for the products that follow.

We’ve been testing face washes and cleansers since this story was first published in 2021. As Men's Health's Grooming Editor, I’m also constantly trying out the latest releases to determine which are worth adding to your rotation. For this update, I considered picks from previous iterations of this roundup, as well as current favorites from fellow Men's Health writers and editors. This ultimately led to me testing over 50 face washes, evaluating their ingredients, feel, consistency, and effectiveness. Below is the culmination of this extensive hands-on research: the ten best face washes for men with any skin type or budget.

For active guys who want a no-nonsense soap that still feels luxurious, this cleanser from Kiehl's delivers. Formulated with hydrating glycerin and squalane—and free of parabens and fragrances—it thoroughly cleanses without stripping moisture. Its powerful ingredients clean and hydrate at the same time, leaving your skin soft, balanced, and primed for the rest of your routine.

Testing Notes: I’ve used Kiehl's cleanser for years and love its ultra-smooth formula that glides easily over my skin. I appreciate that it’s fragrance-free, making it ideal for sensitive skin. Lightweight, gentle, moisturizing, and nourishing, it’s one of the most versatile cleansers I’ve tried—perfect for any skin type. At $16 for 2.5 oz, it isn’t the cheapest option, but it’s still on the affordable side of the market. Because it foams so well, I only need a small amount for a full wash, and one container lasts me about two months with daily use. Overall, Kiehl's Ultra Facial Cleanser remains my go-to everyday face wash, no matter your skin type or budget.

This gel cleanser uses zinc, copper, and magnesium to support the skin’s natural defenses while boosting hydration. Aloe vera then locks in moisture and forms a soothing barrier, while oat calms irritation and comforts sensitive skin. Fragrance-free, it gently removes makeup, sunscreen, and daily buildup without stripping or irritating—even for the most reactive skin.

Testing Notes: I don’t have rosacea, but my skin is prone to redness, so I was excited to see this cleanser approved by the National Rosacea Society—and it didn’t disappoint. Whenever my skin flares up, I use it daily, and within a week or two (depending on severity), the redness quickly calms. Its silky consistency also leaves my skin feeling smooth, balanced, and healthy.

You can’t go wrong with a classic. This Cetaphil cleanser, formulated for combination to oily, sensitive skin, actively removes dirt and excess oil while protecting your skin’s natural barrier. The blend of B vitamins and glycerin nourishes as it cleanses, leaving your face refreshed, balanced, and never tight or dry.

Testing Notes: Cetaphil’s Daily Facial Cleanser delivers incredible value for its price. I love that it packs the same hero ingredients you’d see in pricier formulas, like glycerin and niacinamide, yet it’s gentle enough for even ultra-sensitive skin. It leaves my face feeling clean but never stripped, which makes it easy to reach for every day. My only gripe? I wish the pump dispenser worked more smoothly—it can be frustrating when I’m half-asleep and just want a quick wash.

Long before CeraVe went viral on TikTok, grooming experts swore by the drugstore brand for its high-quality ingredients at budget-friendly prices. A perfect example is this cleanser, packed with hydrating staples like hyaluronic acid and ceramides that strengthen the skin barrier while keeping moisture locked in.

Testing Notes: CeraVe’s Facial Cleanser is one of my go-to budget face washes because it’s easy to find online or in stores, and it simply works. I’ve been using CeraVe since my early 20s, and I can honestly say the formula has never let me down—it removes excess oil and grime without ever causing breakouts.

Shaped like a deodorant stick but designed for your face, this solid soap from Oars and Alps packs charcoal, a buzzy exfoliant that gently scrubs without irritation. I love that even a 1.4-oz container lasts over a month when used daily.

Testing Notes: Oars and Alps’ cleansing stick has become my go-to TSA-friendly face soap for traveling and camping. I love how portable it is and how easily it applies—just like my favorite deodorant—while still exfoliating and removing dirt. It easily fits in my Dopp kit, and I don’t need to worry about it leaking or opening. Plus, my face feels incredibly clean after each use, and a little product really does go a long way.

Finding a TSA-friendly cleanser that doesn't spill is hard. That's where Jaxon Lane's Shake and Wake comes in. It's a powder-to-cream product that gently exfoliates skin and cleans just as well as a liquid cleanser, thanks to a powerful combo of niacinamide, vitamin E, and vitamin C. In other words, it's a Dopp kit must-have.

Testing Notes: The first thing I noticed about this wash was its powdery consistency. What surprised me was how much I liked it—and how often I keep reaching for it, especially when traveling. Similar to Oars and Alps Solid Wash, there is minimal risk of spilling—and even if it did (which I’ve yet to experience), the powder will be far less destructive than liquid.

It feels ultra-gentle on my skin and transforms into a soap-like lather as soon as it hits water. The container is TSA-friendly, tightly sealed, and unlikely to leak, and since it’s powder, even a spill would be minimal and far less messy than a gel.

If you're somebody who loves the smell of the great outdoors, or that irreplaceable feeling felt (and smelt) the early morning after a night of camping, then this face wash is for you. Loaded with skin-boosting natural ingredients like aloe vera, caffeine, and charcoal, Dr. Squatch's face wash exfoliates, refreshes, and cleanses with the best of them.

Testing Notes: With its unique charcoal-backed texture and feel, this wash is one of the most rejuvenating options out there. But what really stands out is its understated, yet still attention-grabbing pine tar scent—subtle enough to avoid clashing with your cologne, but woodsy enough to raise the nostrils in the best way possible.

For those with sensitive or dry skin, there are few (if any) better skincare brands than La Roche-Posay. And the brand's cleanser is a perfect representation of why. Its niacinamide-backed formula is equally gentle and hydrating. Add in other moisturizing winners like glycerin, along with the lack of any skin-aggravating ingredients like heavy fragrances or sulfates, and you have one of the lowest risk, highest reward face washes on the market.

Testing Notes: I have sensitive skin and love this cleanser because it never irritates me. Even if your skin is less reactive, the creamy lather feels amazing during and after each wash. It’s gentle and leaves skin feeling hydrated and healthy.

Talk about value—at under $7 a container, it’s hard to find a more effective, affordable face wash for men than Harry’s. Best known for its stellar shave gear, the brand has quietly expanded into no-nonsense men’s skincare, including standouts like its facial moisturizer. This face wash follows the same formula: it packs low-key hydrators like eucalyptus and peppermint alongside gentle exfoliants like glycerin, delivering a no-BS cleanse that gets the job done without breaking the bank.

Testing Notes: Harry’s hasn’t strayed from its facial-hair roots, as this cleanser doubles as one of the best beard washes, softening whiskers and priming them for trimming or shaving. I also can’t overstate how foamy it gets; it not only strips away dirt and buildup but also makes each (already affordable) container last a long time.

Anyone who struggles with acne knows it takes over your routine, demanding protective, non-invasive, blemish-correcting products at every step. For that crucial first cleanse, Geologie’s new Acne Control Face Wash stands out as the best option. Even though it’s been on the market for barely a year, it has already become a staple for me whenever I’m facing a breakout, thanks to its 2 percent salicylic acid formula and silky-smooth application.

Testing Notes: I still reach for this wash whenever I feel a blemish or breakout coming on. The only drawback is that the gel feels a little stringy at first and needs plenty of water before it foams. Once it does, though, the lather expands quickly, and a dime-sized drop covers my entire face—making each bottle last for months.

Wash your face twice a day—morning and night. Just as important, pay attention to the products you use, avoiding harsh chemicals like sulfates and parabens. Choose a gentle cleanser for everyday use and keep an exfoliating scrub for two or three times a week. Apply the scrub with light pressure—fast, hard, and rough isn’t the answer. Overdoing it can damage your skin and create new problems. And always remember: everyone’s skin type is different. What works for one person might not work for another.

#4895. 8 Best Hotel Mattress Picks for a Five-Star Staycation (2026)

The hotel mattress probably isn't on your vacation itinerary, but it can make or break the trip. A lumpy, unsupportive bed can derail even the most carefully planned getaway. A really good one, though, might become an unexpected highlight—the kind that has you looking forward to bedtime and quietly checking the mattress label before checkout.

Recreating that experience at home doesn't require another plane ticket. Some of our favorite properties, including design-forward waterfront retreats and charming bed-and-breakfasts, put just as much thought into their mattresses as they do their interiors. Many turn to brands like Saatva, Ostermoor, and Casper to outfit their guest rooms; others, like the W Hotels, have signature mattresses you can purchase directly. We've rounded up our favorites, such as options with plush pillow tops, supportive coils, and pressure-relieving foam, to help you bring home the best part of your stay. The room service, unfortunately, is still up to you.

For consistency, all the prices reflect queen-size mattresses.

A stay at the Ritz-Carlton is typically reflected by its refined, elegant bedrooms. The property’s eponymous bed invites the same feeling. At 14 inches, it’s a higher-profile mattress that can help make the bed the centerpiece of the room. One of the standout qualities is its coil system, as it includes 900-plus individual springs for great edge support to help keep the sides from sagging as well as promote motion isolation—a necessary factor for couples who don’t want to sense each other’s every move.

Serta is one of the most well-known mattress manufacturers for high-end hotels, such as the Waldorf-Astoria. While many luxury properties feature custom beds from the namesake brand, it doesn’t mean you can’t shop at popular retailers such as Amazon. You’d never guess it, but this premium bed is priced under $500 (making it the most affordable on our list). While Serta offers memory foam and hybrid versions of its beds, this pillow-top innerspring mattress has been a favorite in our shopping writer Julia Harrison’s space, and she says it lives up to its “Five-Star” name.

It’s filled with three zones of coil support that keep her free of back and neck problems, and the quilted cover gives her something soft to dream about each night. “I’m really not one for pomp and frills in my mattress—I’m a firm believer that a good mattress has very little going on besides a somewhat plush top to keep you from feeling any sort of spring mechanism going on inside,” she says in her mattress review. “I instantly slept well on this mattress I think because it’s quite simply: a great mattress.” Bonus: It’s a mattress-in-a-box, so it can fit easily through narrow doors and hallways once it’s delivered, and inflate to its full size in less than a day’s time after unboxing, according to Harrison. Just in case you’re on the fence, it comes with a 100-day sleep trial so you can really see if it’s right for you before committing.

The Six Bells Countryside Inn opened its doors in the bucolic Hudson Valley in 2025, and it’s already earned two Michelin Keys. In each of the 11 carefully and whimsically designed bedrooms at this retreat, you’ll find handcrafted mattresses and bedding from New York-born brand Ostermoor. Dating back to 1853, Ostermoor’s mattresses have a storied history. The beds have innovated to foam and pocketed coil inner layers and designer covers in recent years, and we can prove they’re worth the splurge.

“From the moment I plopped down on the mattress, I was amazed by how comfortable and supportive it was,” shares contributor Zoë Sessums. “It strikes a perfect balance between spring and cushion—just the right amount of give without ever feeling too soft. I consistently wake up feeling rested and supported.” Firm without feeling rigid, this mattress looks as good as it feels, too. “The tufted top, the blue and white ticking pattern, the hand-stitched details—it feels like a piece of luxury furniture, not just a place to sleep,” Sessums adds, later writing, “I would recommend this to someone who values design and craftsmanship as much as comfort.”

Saatva has found its way into charming bed-and-breakfasts and boutique retreats across the country, including Pasadena's historic Bissell House (an 1887 Victorian filled with antique furnishings) and the Cornell Inn in the Berkshires (known for its colorful, individually designed guest rooms). You can bring that same inviting comfort home with the Saatva Classic, which comes with a plush three-inch Euro pillow top, a responsive dual-coil system, and targeted lumbar support. “It’s firm (which I prefer), regulates temperature well, and is extremely durable,” our tester Erin Kaplan, vice president of communications at Conde Nast, says. “I alternate between sleeping on my side and sleeping on my stomach, and this mattress is great for both positions.”

Choose from three firmness levels—plush soft, luxury firm, or firm—, eight different sizes, and two mattress heights to find your ideal fit. Feeling extra? Saatva also offers two adjustable bases that elevate your head and feet at the touch of a button, including a premium Plus model for an even more indulgent breakfast in bed. A 365-night trial gives you plenty of time to sleep on your decision before committing.

At 1 Hotel Brooklyn Bridge, even the beds have a view. Sweeping views of the Manhattan skyline set the scene, with reclaimed wood floors, rich leather headboards, and locally crafted details like crate-inspired closets and Fresnel glass light fixtures bringing warmth and character to the rooms. With custom Keetsa mattresses in every room, you might find yourself hitting snooze despite the spectacular view.

Back at home, the Keetsa Pillow Plus offers its own take on hotel-worthy comfort. It's something of a Goldilocks mattress: not too soft, not too firm, but just right. A three-inch pillow top combines body-contouring memory foam with responsive comfort foam to help cushion pressure points, and a soft, moisture-wicking cover designed to keep overheating at bay. Individually wrapped coils provide cushioning and support while minimizing motion transfer, so even if your bedmate tosses and turns, you can stay blissfully unaware.

When husband-and-wife duo Ely and Danielle Franko transformed a dated Catskills ski hostel into The Henson, a 16-room boutique hotel, they had a pretty good idea of what makes a great night's sleep. The couple painstakingly restored the property themselves, filling its rooms with vintage furniture, locally sourced finds, and hand-applied wallpaper. But when it came to mattresses, they didn't have to look far for inspiration: They chose the same Casper Dream Hybrid they sleep on at home. In fact, they loved it so much that they insisted on king-size mattresses in every room, even the smallest ones. The hybrid design combines responsive springs with breathable foam and three zones of support that help keep your spine aligned. Its medium feel is meant to offer a little give without leaving you sinking into the mattress, making it a crowd-pleasing choice for your own guest room. After all, the best hosts know a good night's sleep is part of the hospitality.

Hot sleepers, here’s a mattress for you. The Four Season’s signature mattress features a couple of core cooling bed qualities: proprietary cooling gel foam layers with channeled designs that promote airflow throughout the mattress, as well as a patented DualCool top layer that draws heat and moisture away from the body and keeps the bed fresh with its antimicrobial properties. The cooling mattress is designed for sleepers who need extra structure on their bed. This posh number has targeted support for the lower back area and zeroes in on alignment regardless of your sleep style.

The W Hotels are widely popular because of the bold design across the properties worldwide. To mirror this aesthetic, you can cover the brand’s mattress with colorful bedding to let your personal style shine. When it comes to the bed itself, it is defined by a plush top quilted damask design to ease side sleepers into a peaceful slumber. It’s made for people who need extra support too, though, including an individually-wrapped coil system, five-zone support system, and comfort layers for added cushioning and pressure relief.

Which Kind of Mattress Do Five-Star Hotels Use?

Most luxury hotels use hybrid mattresses in their suites to strike the right balance of softness and support, thanks to pocketed coils and layers of foam. These are also typically medium-firm mattresses since a plush mattress can be uncomfortable for some sleep positions like stomach sleepers. Ultra-firm beds are often too stiff for side sleeping and may not align with guests' expectations who are looking for soft mattresses to sink into on their vacations.

If you want to refresh your mattress without the hefty price tag of buying a new one, a mattress topper or featherbed could be a solid transitional pick. The Ritz-Carlton and W Hotels promote one made with white duck feathers, Mandarin Oriental’s exclusive topper comprises white goose feathers, Waldorf Astoria beds feature a down-alternative fill, and Marriott’s selection is polyester.

There’s no one-size-fits-all here, so it really comes down to your preferred loftiness and weight. Duck and goose feathers are heavier than others fills, though duck is slightly less fluffy and won’t trap heat as well. Down-alternatives, like polyester, are more allergen-friendly and “a good option for those who prefer to be vegan in their home,” Danielle Trotter, the former textiles technical designer at West Elm, previously shared.

What Is the Thickness of a Hotel Mattress?

Hotel mattresses usually average 12 inches in thickness. This makes it easier to hop in and out of bed, especially when using a box spring that can add extra height. Plus, it prevents the need for deep pocket sheets.

How Can I Recreate the Hotel Bed Experience at Home?

We’ve explored the entire topic on how to make your bedroom feel like a hotel, and aside from finding a new bed with a medium-firm feel, we’ve learned that percale sheets and down pillows are pretty much a must to complete the setup. When it comes to the former, hotel sheets are usually made with organic cotton percale because the fabric looks and feels crisp, giving that refined aesthetic a boutique stay is known for. Usually a 200 thread count is a good rule of thumb to look out for since this means there’s plenty of airflow between the threads for a breathable feel. Hotel pillows are usually filled with down feathers since they’re so lofty and soft, but a down alternative is just as good in case you’re an allergy-prone sleeper (just look for materials like hypoallergenic gel fibers since they’re known for being squishy without falling flat, just like a feather-filled pillow).

What Is the Difference Between Memory Foam and Latex?

Traditional memory foam has a body-contouring effect that allows your body to sink into your mattress, reducing motion transfer (a must for bedmates!). Meanwhile, latex foam offers more responsiveness (or bounce) and overall support. As Neslihan Ozdemir, founder of Girl on the Mattress, previously told AD, latex also holds up well over time and is temperature-regulating. Latex foam mattresses (and some memory foam options) are certified organic, making them eco-friendly foam picks, too.

Known as the most common mattress type, innerspring mattresses feature a bed of coils. There’s quite a range to these mattresses: Basic versions have a grid of steel coils, while premier options have a pillow top and pocketed coil technology, meaning each coil is individually wrapped to help with motion isolation. Ozdemir added that innerspring is best for people who sleep on the edge of the bed or are heavier in weight. If you prefer a more plush mattress, but still want the support of those coils, consider a hybrid mattress, which is layered with soft foam.

#4892. The 7 Best Portable Basketball Hoops and Systems for Any Yard or Driveway

If you want to ball out at home, these are the hoops for you.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

If you live by the "ball is life" moniker and you need to be able to play at home, a portable basketball hoop is a must. Portable basketball hoops don't require you to perform manual labor like digging a huge hole in the ground and pouring concrete, nor do they cost over a thousand bucks. Another plus to going portable? You can store your hoop come winter, thus lengthening its lifespan. It’s also a solid option for those who don't have the time, money, or space to install an in-ground option but still wanna toss their basketball shoes on and shoot around a bit quickly.

"I feel like the portable hoop is what transformed me into who I am," NBA shooting coach Chris Matthews (a.k.a. Lethal Shooter) says. "My cousin Justin and I would play on the portable hoop at his house when we couldn't make it to the playground. He had a garage light, and we would shoot all night."

You can make memories like that in whatever space you have for the court. But don't get caught buying a hoop that’s a waste of money. Not all hoops are the same, so we’re here to cut through the noise. Here are some of the best options we came up with.

Spalding makes a handful of portable goals, but the Momentous EZ is our favorite due to its value-driven price and ease of assembly. Spalding notes it takes about 30 minutes to put together. We found it took just over that time when following the instructions, which makes it the easiest goal to assemble in our book.

As Matthews notes, "The more portable a basketball hoop is, the better, so that everyone can move it. That's one reason I like the models from Spalding."

As for the materials in the hoop, the Momentous EZ comes with an acrylic backboard in either 50- or 54-inch sizing. You can also choose between a clear view back, an H-frame, or a steel H-frame (for added support and durability). We chose the steel H-frame to help prevent backboard damage. The theory behind the H-frame is that it should help absorb stress when someone dunks or hangs on the rim.

There's a hand crank for adjusting the height of the goal (simple to use if you have kids or if you want to do a driveway dunk contest). The base is wide and supportive and will hold up to 26 gallons of water or sand. If you're looking for a premium goal that won't set you back a thousand dollars, there's nothing better than this pick. Start here in your search. You won't regret it.

More: The 6 Best Basketballs for Indoor Games and Street Hoops

If you are looking for a portable goal that won't break the bank, this top-selling $250 model is worth a look. It's made to adjust to a wide range of height, from 4.8 feet to 10 feet. This means it appeals to everyone from small kids to adults. One cool idea you can do with this goal is you can lower it to its 4-foot setting and position it up against an in-ground pool—something other goals in this guide don't have a low enough range to make it suitable for pool hoops.

The biggest qualm about this one is the polycarbonate backboard. It won't last as long as acrylic, and you should expect a few good years out of it with a slight decline in bounce as it braves the changing of the seasons. One way to help preserve this goal, though, is to store it inside whenever possible to avoid weathering.

Lifetime is another brand that churns out long-lasting portable goals. This one is similar to the Spalding Momentous EZ with a wide acrylic backboard. The base is also just as sturdy as the Spalding EZ, and it has an ability to hold up to 35 gallons of water or sand. The downside of this goal to the Spalding EZ is it's not as fast of a setup, so you do need to lock in for at least two hours to get it up.

The upside? That would be the 4 extra inches of backboard, the reinforced rim, and the hand crank adjustment. The rim is thicker and outfitted with steel springs, which makes it a lot more capable for handling dunks. The hand crank makes adjusting the goal from 7.5 feet to 10 feet smoother and easier than the turning hand crank on the Spalding EZ goal.

The Spalding has the easier setup and price, but Lifetime has a few premium features that will make competitive play more fun.

The FORZA Adjustable Basketball Hoop and Post System earns its place as a “Best Adjustable Hoop for Growing Players” thanks to its flexible height settings and portable design. Built for both kids learning their first shots and adults looking for competitive backyard games, the hoop adjusts from youth-friendly heights to regulation size, making it a long-term investment rather than something your kids quickly outgrow. Its wheeled base also makes it easy to move across driveways or patios, adding convenience for families who want flexibility.

Designed for indoor or outdoor use, the hoop features a sturdy base and adjustable frame that can accommodate players of different ages and skill levels. This versatile hoop can come out when you're hosting weekend family games or serious practice sessions, but be stored when not in use. There are also optional upgrades available.

This model from IE Sports will help save you some cash while still providing decent play. Its made with a 44-inch polycarbonate backboard, which is great when it comes to saving money. The base and frame are similar in design to the Awii Sports option, so there's no worries on durability here.

Like mentioned prior, we don't really like the hand crank for adjusting the height; this goal has one. You've probably noticed the unique mini trampoline this goal comes with so you can pass the ball to yourself. We think it's an awesome feature, as it maximizes solo practice by allowing you to work on passing and catch-and-shoot drills. Overall, this goal is reliable, well-priced, and comes with a fun feature.

Remember how fun mini hoops are? This goal takes mini hoops to a whole other level with an adjustable height pole (up to 7 feet) and a sturdy base. Sure you could buy a cheap sub-$100 full size goal for your kids to play with, but for a similar price you get a much better build and a whole lot of fun.

Position it up to your pool for water mini hoops. Bring it down to your basement or put it in the garage for winter mini hoops. You get the point.

The Huupe Mini Hoop is the perfect nostalgia pick for any guy, regardless of age. It is quite literally the most portable hoop on our list, with the ability to be tossed on any door. This smart hoop has a wide variety of virtual games you can enjoy. The hoop comes with some heft, namely from the technology, which allows you to test your shot against others online, or even watch your favorite streaming apps.

"I think that mini hoops like the Huupe are another great option for families that don't have room in their garage or a driveway," Matthews says. "It's a great way to have kids to get energy out during the day, even when the weather is not ideal. They are easy to install, too."

In any case, it's easily installed using the classic over-the-door mount. You can also wall mount, but you need to buy those parts separately. There are special sensors throughout the device, which follow your shot as well as your distance from the hoop. This means it can reliably track your shot so you can get better after every game. One of our testers even said, "I enjoyed using this hoop to shoot around with my toddler daughter, and when I just wanted to play around a little bit by myself, it was awesome to get to watch the NBA playoffs on the screen as I shot."

Chris Matthews (aka Lethal Shooter) is a world-renowned shooting coach to NBA stars like Jaylen Brown, Dwight Howard, and Anthony Davis, and WNBA star Candice Parker.

Having spent countless hours as kids growing up playing pickup games in driveways, we know a thing or two about a solid portable basketball hoop. Men's Health Fitness and Commerce Editor Charles Thorp, NASM, has played lots of basketball and helped us dial in on the proper picks for this guide. Considering all those firsthand experiences led us to find the best of the best. Factors like backboard material, adjustability, and special design notes were considered in our selection process. We also took into account price, as some basketball goals provide a better overall value than others.

In addition, we also consulted world-renowned basketball shooting coach Chris Matthews (a.k.a. Lethal Shooter) on what makes for a good portable hoop. Our guide below represents our top picks, all approved by Matthews, of portable basketball hoops that will actually last for years to come. Keep scrolling to learn more.

Not every hoop is going to have the same adjustability in terms of how low or high you can raise it. This is crucial if you have little ones and want the whole family to partake in the fun. It’s also a great way to put on a dunk contest if you still have the bunnies, too. There are also different mechanisms built for adjusting, such as a hand crank, a telescoping pole, pneumatic assist, or a gas spring.

The types of materials used directly impact the long-term durability of your hoop. The two types of backboard materials to know about for portable basketball goals are acrylic and polycarbonate (there's also glass, but glass is used for professional backboards and is extremely rare on portable ones). Polycarbonate is going to be cheaper, but the tradeoff is that exposure to weather and UV light will make the backboard brittle and rigid over time. Acrylic is typically more expensive, but the benefit is that it's better suited for exposure to weather and UV light (acrylic is not affected by UV light like polycarbonate), plus you get a more responsive bounce.

Basketball rims are not all created equal. If you’ve ever been to a park court, you know what we mean—one slightly off shot and your ball rockets across the street. There are a few common materials you’ll see: steel and double-rimmed steel, powder-coated rims, and occasionally composite or plastic. You’ll also see that there are breakaway rims, standard, and flex.

To keep a portable basketball hoop in place, you'll need to fill its base with something. Most portable goals hold about 35 gallons, and you can either go with water or sand. We prefer sand because it dissipates well. Sand is also denser than water, so filling the base with sand is wiser for a more secure hold. However, choosing water makes it easier to empty the base and refill, making it easier to maneuver, especially if you need to move elsewhere in your driveway (or take it to your neighbor's for a friendly pickup game).

If you're curious about how much weight you need to keep your goal in place, a safe number is around 300 to 450 pounds. It sounds like a lot, but if you want to be safe and protect your goal, then more weight is always worth adding. And keep in mind that they all include wheels attached to the base to move them more easily. If you want to eliminate the labor of filling the base full, you can fill it to a point and then stack sandbags on top of the back of the goal to keep it in place. It won't be the most pleasing to look at, but it will allow you to move the goal around more easily.

Paying more gets you a better playing experience, especially when it comes to a wide acrylic backboard. A wider backboard makes it easier to shoot bank shots and perform layups, and the acrylic material will be much more responsive and last longer. A more expensive goal might also come with better wheels for moving the goal. Keep in mind a portable basketball hoop won't be as deluxe as an in-ground one, but you can get pretty dang close.

A regulation backboard is typically 48 inches tall by 72 inches wide. Most portable hoops have a 48-inch height, but there's a variance on width. While 72 inches is fun to play on due to the full ability to shoot bank shots and layups, a driveway goal doesn't need to be that wide.

Look to a 50-inch or 54-inch width. Anything under 50 is fine; however, you will lose space to shoot bank shots and layups. The benefit to buying a goal with a smaller backboard, though, is that you save money (they're almost always cheaper).

The easiest way to store a portable basketball goal is to lower the rim to its lowest setting, tarp it, then roll it into a garage or shed. Some basketball hoops can be disassembled (or at least partially disassembled), but that process can be pretty annoying. Make sure to drain any water from the base to avoid it freezing and expanding the plastic of the base.

Some of the high-end Spalding portable goals can partially disassemble for storage (not the Spalding EZ we recommend, though). You can take out bolts at the middle of the goal, and the backboard will fold down, thus helping store it in a garage or shed with a low ceiling.

#4888. 7 Best Writing Desks That Are Furniture Chameleons (2026)

Regardless of whether you have a home office or not, a good writing desk is a versatile piece of furniture to have on hand. Unlike a secretary desk, which is usually equipped with a drop-front panel or concealed compartments, this type of desk has a streamlined surface and open-leg construction, making it best suited for pen-and-paper tasks. In other words, it’s less intrusive style-wise since it’s not designed to have a million compartments for cable management or bulky drawers to stash old bills.

The design options feel endless in this furniture category. You can try a larger, minimal silhouette with a slender drawer or two if you’re a creative like TV writer Mike Gauyo, who spends hours behind a writing desk in a Los Angeles studio. Or you can opt for a vintage desk to bring lived-in character to your interiors, like the styles in this A-frame Catskills cabin and Southampton, New York, enclave. Because the silhouettes are so adaptable, many can easily work as entryway console tables, dressing tables, and even sideboards to hold extra plates and silverware after all your dinner parties.

All in all, this desk setup encourages peaceful moments rooted in intention, and it might speed up your to-do list. Now is the time to knock out those holiday cards or try your hand at writing a novel.

The clean lines and neutral tones make this less-is-more desk our favorite for minimalists. Even though it has a simple look, it’s customizable—with three top colors and two wire base layers available—to help you style it perfectly for your space. Once you position it in the right spot, spread out your paperwork across the roomy, scratch-and-stain-resistant surface. (No more coffee mug rings!)

Add a bit of Wizard of Oz magic to your home office with this green, spacious desk. The emerald hue has been trending over the last few years, and designers often use it throughout interiors since it represents serenity—not a bad option for an office space. The vibrant color and petite size can also work as an accent piece, should you need something more than a console near the stairs in a foyer.

See how the wood grain detail comes through the honey oak finish. This and the notched leg detail give this McGee & Co. desk a heritage quality. We can picture this beauty tucked in on a landing nook in a cabin. Add a table lamp with bespoke detail, like a linen pleated shade, and you’ve got storybook design.

Leave it to social media star Emma Chamberlain to invite her cool-girl vibes into your home. At just under 40 pounds, this gem is ideal for a studio space or a teeny spare bedroom. Picture it in front of a little window with a cute vase of posies. Stash a journal in the petite drawer to help you carve out a little spot to daydream.

When you want your writing desk to double as a showpiece, look no further than Lulu and Georgia’s Maksim design. Stacked curves flank each side, as if the desk were a functional sculpture. The acacia wood is stained black, giving the piece more of a moody, contemporary look. Its larger footprint, a 52-inch-wide surface, provides plenty of space for desk accessories—like a black leather and wood mousepad to match the modern style.

A work surface or a mirage? The all-glass Ebern Designs writing table speaks to idiosyncratic design thanks to its minimalist, waterfall look. Should you feel like the style needs a bit more visual interest, consider pairing it with a desk chair outfitted in mohair upholstery or jewel tones.

Twist-in-leg construction is a perk when assembling an office desk that doesn’t come with white-glove delivery. The telltale midcentury-modern silhouette with angled legs and a sleek storage drawer means this style fits in with most contemporary furnishings. If you want to soften up the look, drape a throw blanket over the chair.

#4887. Former CAKE team is back in the kitchen with a new electric motorcycle

If the new ReBake Abler electric motorcycle looks like it might share a bit of DNA with Sweden’s dearly departed CAKE, there’s a good reason for that.

ReBake Motors has officially unveiled its first electric two-wheeler at EICMA 2026 in Milan, introducing the Abler as a highly modular, utility-focused electric moped and light motorcycle.

Behind the new Swedish company is founder and CEO Karl Ytterborn, who spent eight years at CAKE from its founding in 2016 through 2024. CAKE famously built some of the most interesting minimalist electric motorcycles and utility bikes on the market before ultimately collapsing after failing to secure additional funding. Ytterborn says ReBake is intended to apply many of the lessons learned during that experience, while eliminating unnecessary cost and complexity.

Its chunky 42mm aluminum tube frame isn’t just a styling exercise. ReBake designed it as a mounting system, allowing cargo accessories to attach directly to the frame at multiple locations. That means riders can configure the bike for everything from carrying groceries and passengers to more serious utility duties.

There are two versions. The Abler45 is an EU L1e-B moped with a 45 km/h (28 mph) top speed, 4 kW nominal motor and 5.12 kW peak output. It starts at €3,990 including VAT.

The €4,990 Abler80 steps up to the A1 light motorcycle category, increasing nominal power to 6.14 kW and peak power to 7.68 kW while pushing the top speed beyond 80 km/h (50 mph). Both versions use a direct-drive rear hub motor.

Energy comes from removable 2 kWh lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries weighing 17 kg (37.5 lb) apiece. The Abler45 comes standard with one battery but can carry two, while the Abler80 includes two for 4 kWh of total capacity. With both batteries, ReBake claims up to 160 km (99 miles) of low-speed urban range on the Abler45 or 114 km (71 miles) on the Abler80. Each battery can be charged either on or off the bike from a normal 230V outlet, reaching a full charge in four hours.

The rest of the hardware includes 14-inch cast wheels, 140mm of front suspension travel, dual rear shocks, front and rear disc brakes with combined braking, regenerative braking, and full LED lighting.

Perhaps more interesting than any individual specification, though, is simply seeing another Swedish electric motorcycle startup emerge from CAKE’s ashes.

CAKE demonstrated that there was plenty of appetite for unconventional, lightweight electric motorcycles. Unfortunately, it also demonstrated just how difficult it is to turn that enthusiasm into a sustainable business.

ReBake appears to be getting another crack at that equation – this time with eight years’ worth of lessons already baked in.

#4885. Joseph Dirand Joins Forces with Peter Brant and Stephanie Seymour Brant to Reimagine a Historic 1920s Palm Beach Mansion

It began with a chance encounter and a phone call. The French architect Joseph Dirand was walking into a restaurant in New York when he ran into an old friend, the art dealer Tico Mugrabi. Dirand mentioned that he was flying to Palm Beach the next day and his friend lit up. Mugrabi pulled out his phone and made a call. “Peter, my friend Joseph is coming to Palm Beach tomorrow,” Dirand recalls him saying. “You have to meet this guy.” The following day Dirand was sitting across from Peter Brant, the fabled industrialist and publisher, and his wife, Stephanie Seymour Brant, one of the defining supermodels of her generation, in their new home. The Brants had owned the house for only a few days, and it marked the opening of a new chapter for the couple.

The Brants in front of Warhol’s White Disaster (White Car Crash 19 Times), 1963, in the great room. Jean Prouvé coffee table; sofa and chairs by Pierre Jeanneret.

Marc Newson’s aluminum Lockheed Lounge, a Tower Cabinet by Ettore Sottsass, and a Trapeze table by Jean Prouvé all stand in the loggia.

A Végétale mirror by Claude Lalanne reflects Untitled (Richard Prince and Cindy Sherman), 1980, and a 1930s settee by Jean-Michel Frank.

A pair of bespoke Philippe Anthonioz floor lamps Flank Jonathan Horowitz’s Self-portrait in “Mirror #1” (Kevin), 2012.

Brown Jordan chaise longues under umbrellas by Business & Pleasure Co. stand poolside.

There is something quintessentially American in how quickly it all unfolded, and for Dirand, it meant meeting a man he had long admired. As an inquisitive young designer he had pored over photographs of Brant’s earlier homes, and one image had stayed with him: It showed a Jean Prouvé desk beneath a Jean-Michel Basquiat painting, captured at a time when almost no one thought to set French postwar design against contemporary art. “For me, Peter was a kind of collector’s hero,” says Dirand.

Brant’s eye for art and design was formed early. His father loved classical art and considered even Picasso “way too modern,” but on family ski trips to Switzerland the teenage Brant got to know the Zurich dealer Bruno Bischofberger, who subsequently introduced him to Leo Castelli, and the two titans of the art world became the young Brant’s mentors. Brant then bought his first Andy Warhol painting in 1966, and by the time Warhol’s business manager, Fred Hughes, introduced them in November 1968, he already owned about seven of them. Warhol and Brant would go on to become close friends for the remainder of the artist’s life.

In a corner of the Great Room, Roy Lichtenstein’s The Refrigerator, 1962, faces a 1960 copper hanging cabinet by Paul Evans. a 1934 plaster vase by Alberto Giacometti sits on A Joseph Dirand Edition Iseo Gold coffee table. 1950s Hirondelles wall light by Jean Royère; pair of 1958 Diego Giacometti armchairs.

Warhol’s 1975 portrait of Murray Brant (Brant’s father) commands a wall of the paneled study. Direction armchair and Présidence desk by Jean Prouvé; Ettore Sottsass hanging lamp.

Artworks in the entrance hall include, from left, a Massangis stone lion-head fountain feature by Harumi Klossowska de Rola, 2022; Andy Warhol’s Self Portrait (Green), 1964; a Klossowska de Rola wolf sculpture; and Richard Prince’s Nurses’ Dormitory, 2002. The sanded Ceppo di Gré stone modular console is by Dirand.

In the primary bedroom, George Condo’s 2004 portrait of Stephanie Seymour Brant hangs above a 1946 Charlotte Perriand sideboard on which stands an enameled earthenware lamp by Roger Capron. A Jean Prouvé Bridge armchair joins an Ours Polaire chair and sofa by Jean Royère around Prouvé’s Tripod coffee table.

An exterior view of the 1926 Addison Mizner residence

Few people then saw Warhol’s work the way Brant did. When he hung his first Marilyn at home, visitors were shocked: “People would come to my house and think, This is the worst thing I’ve ever seen. In the 1960s, he says, you could count the serious collectors of Pop art “on three hands.”

His rule, he says, is to collect “something that was in style that’s out of style,” though never as speculation. Between their holdings and those of the Brant Foundation, which he established in 1996 to promote the education and appreciation of contemporary art and design, the collection now numbers more than 3,000 works, and he has never bought for a particular wall. What he misses in many newer collections is any sense of the person behind them. “You can see right away that this guy had a great adviser,” he says, “but there’s no madness in the collection. Every collection should have some madness.”

Carlo Mollino’s Tipo B side chair rests beneath Jean-Michel Basquiat’s Per Capita, 1981.

A painting by Glenn Ligon and a stool by Shiro Kuramata in Brant’s bath

Seymour Brant and Brant in the great room

Brant has shared much of his collecting journey with Seymour Brant, whom he married in 1995. She has built a collection of her own: Her passion is clothing rather than paintings, and she has pursued it with the same scholarship and the same sharp eye as her husband. She was a close friend of the legendary couturier Azzedine Alaïa and has one of the most significant holdings of his work, alongside historic couture that Dirand describes as extraordinary. Where Brant is the storyteller, Seymour Brant is the quieter presence, though Dirand is clear that she was integral to every decision. Her collecting has even changed the way Brant sees his own. “It’s not a dress in a closet,” he says. “It’s a piece of art, and it mixes with art.”

Brant has spent some 50 years in the Palm Beach area, first as a polo player. He and Seymour Brant had no need for a new home there—they loved the one they had as their children grew up. But when Collado Hueco, a home by Addison Mizner, the architect who defined 1920s Palm Beach, came on the market in 2020, the collector in him took over. “It was a piece of history,” Dirand says. “For him, there was no choice.” Designed in 1924 for the American businessman Paul Moore, it is one of Mizner’s boldest and most unusual houses.

In a hall, a 1974 Diego Giacometti bench sits in front of Jean-Michel Basquiat’s Untitled (Sugar Ray Robinson), 1982. The curtain rods are by Julian Schnabel.

Warhol’s The Kiss (Bela Lugosi), 1964, and a 1947 Alexandre Noll mahogany armchair in a corner of the primary bedroom. Philippe Anthonioz hanging light; Jean Prouvé tripod coffee table; Jean Royère Ours Polaire sofa.

John Currin’s Constance Towers, 2009, presides over Seymour Brant’s dressing room. Furniture includes an Ambassador chair and Éléphanteau sofa, both by Jean Royère.

In the great room, a plaster bas-relief, Support, and a carved-stone console by Alberto Giacometti are flanked by a pair of Éléphanteau chairs by Jean Royère. In the foreground is a Fondation Maeght chair by Diego Giacometti.

The house presented Dirand with a real puzzle. Asymmetrical, it spreads across multiple wings, varying from one to three levels. The main entertaining rooms had retained their original character, while the entrance and stair hall were dark and enclosed. Dirand set out to let the sunlight that moves across the house reach every part of the interior as much as possible. The collection shaped Dirand’s approach too. With so many treasured works coming into the house, the team wanted to ensure they would be protected against anything the unpredictable Florida weather could bring. What began as a renovation became, in Dirand’s words, “a reconstruction saving the historical.” Rather than demolishing and starting again, the team kept the historic walls standing, reinforced every one of them, and dug beneath to take the foundations deeper. New hurricane-proof windows were set into concrete frames, the roof was removed and rebuilt, and the original tiles and the patina of the plaster fireplace were carefully preserved. The project took about four years. Throughout, Dirand immersed himself in Mizner’s doors, ceilings, and patterns so that the new rooms would be a true homage rather than a copy.

Early on, Brant handed Dirand two thick binders, one of artworks and one of design pieces. “This is what you can use,” he said. A few days later, on holiday with his family, Dirand spread every page across the floors. “I was walking on the paper,” he says. It reversed the usual order in which the architect designs the rooms and the art arrives afterward. Here the collection came first, though never rigidly, because “a collection is also something that is alive.”

A Diego Giacometti bench and A Jean Royère Liane six-branch floor lamp in a hall

A chair and floor lamp by Diego Giacometti stand next to the fireplace in the great room.

Jean-Michel Basquiat’s Per Capita, 1981, commands a wall of the loggia. Ours Polaire chair and Yo-Yo side table, both by Royère.

A family photo and fragrance bottles line up on a windowsill in Seymour Brant’s bath.

Warhol’s Big Campbell’s Soup Can with Can Opener (Vegetable), 1962, hangs in the stairwell, which also features a Jacques Adnet wall light.

At the heart of the home are two main spaces, the great room and the loggia, which are perhaps the spaces that both Dirand and Brant are most proud of. The great room is centered around a monumental fireplace that has the grandeur of a castle. Commanding one wall is a rare carved-stone console by Alberto Giacometti, nearly three meters high and crowned with a bas-relief of a female figure, made for Jean-Michel Frank’s important 1938 commission for the Born family in Argentina. It was one of a pair, and Dirand says no one knows where the other is today. Beside the fireplace hangs Warhol’s 1963 White Disaster (White Car Crash 19 Times), one of Brant’s most recent and important acquisitions; he had wanted a Car Crash painting since the ’60s. Prouvé furniture from Brazzaville, weathered by the Congo climate, sits amid Native American and African objects, and at the center of it all is a mirror polish copper table Dirand designed himself to reflect Giacometti’s bird vase and the fireplace behind it. Brant calls the table a masterpiece.

Art in the main entrance includes, from left, pieces by Jean-Michel Basquiat, Richard Prince and Cindy Sherman, and Brice Marden. Furniture includes an Ours Polaire Chair and sofa and a kidney-shaped coffee table, all by Jean Royère, and a Charlotte Perriand stool. a 1936 Jean-Michel Frank settee stands in the background.

A glimpse into the primary bedroom, where a Jean-Michel Frank table lamp sits atop a bedside table.

A wall niche holds a 2023 ibis sculpture by Harumi Klossowska de Rola

The loggia is lighter and more playful, and its original black, yellow, and turquoise tiled floor and Egyptian-style column capitals offer a glimpse of Mizner at his most adventurous. One of the most prominent works hanging in the room is a monumental 1981 Basquiat painting, Per Capita, which Brant bought from Annina Nosei’s memorial show for the artist. At the center of the room stands an Ettore Sottsass Tower Cabinet, designed in the early 1960s, which Dirand admits he didn’t understand at first, until Brant showed him exactly how to place it. Now he can’t imagine the room without it.

Upstairs, Dirand took down walls so that the primary bedroom runs the full width of the house, capturing light from sunrise over the ocean to sunset over the garden. In Seymour Brant’s bathroom, Estremoz marble walls are carved to evoke curtains, and beyond it lies her dressing room, an intimate boudoir. Brant’s bathroom, by contrast, is a marquetry of white and gray marble built around a pair of Glenn Ligon paintings. Dirand calls the room “minimalist ornamental.”

A 2023 flamingo sculpture by Harumi Klossowska de Rola (one of a pair) stands on the terrace.

In Seymour Brant’s bath, François-Xavier Lalanne’s Singe II, 1999, sits between a stool by Diego Giacometti and a bespoke bench by Philippe Anthonioz.

Every piece in the house comes with a story, and Dirand heard many of them over years of breakfasts, lunches, and dinners with the couple. “Every single piece could be a book,” he says. During those conversations, the collaboration between Brant and Dirand grew into a close friendship. Brant’s other great passion is horse racing, and his formidable stable has included Sottsass, the 2020 winner of the Prix de l’Arc de Triomphe, Europe’s most prestigious race. One day, Brant called Dirand with news: Sottsass had a son, a young thoroughbred already winning races of his own. He had named him Dirand.
